It is difficult because more ambiguous distributions demand more model capacity, larger embeddings, more fitting steps, and they amplify token-sampling noise, so the model is harder to train accurately on them [1]. A related result is that with K-fold ambiguity, neural networks first learn the marginal distribution and can sit at a loss plateau set by the ambiguity before later acquiring the full conditional, with gradient noise and learning-rate settings affecting how long that plateau lasts [2].

Several papers also show that models tend to collapse toward the most probable or dominant interpretation instead of matching the desired distribution, which makes highly ambiguous or probabilistic outputs especially hard to learn and sample correctly [3, 7, 8].
